title: Honnō-ji: Did Mitsuhide Shout It? 245 Years of Rewrites｜Curio Archive
description:
“The enemy is at Honnō-ji” is Japan's most famous line of betrayal, yet not one record left from that night in 1582 contains it. So who wrote it?
For anyone who loves Japan's Sengoku era, or wonders how a famous quote gets written.

This episode follows the records in the order they appeared. The Shinchō Kōki says Mitsuhide told his whole army they would march via Yamazaki to Settsu. Ōmura Yūko's Koretō Taijiki only records that they set out. The missionary Luís Fróis reported that the soldiers were told it was a review of troops, and some thought the target was Ieyasu. Honjō Sōemon, a veteran who marched in the column, recalled in 1640: “We thought it was Ieyasu.” The Kawasumi Taikōki says that near Kyoto, Saitō Toshimitsu told each unit to aim for the grove at Honnō-ji. The words that truly survive from that night are Nobunaga's: “Zehi ni oyobazu.”

The earliest written form we have found is in the Oda Nobunaga-fu, compiled by Hayashi Razan and his son on the shogun's orders (presented in 1641): soldiers ask at Ōeyama, and only then does Mitsuhide answer. Nearly two hundred years later, Rai San'yō's Nihon Gaishi (1827) moved the scene to the Katsura River, with Mitsuhide pointing his whip east and shouting the line himself. From the Meiji era on, that became the version everyone remembers, and even a Japanese idiom.

We read Fróis's report and the Kawasumi Taikōki through later quotations; the veteran's memoir is of unclear origin, so we treat it as one man's memory. “Earliest” means only as far as we have found. Why Mitsuhide rose against Nobunaga is still not settled. Dates in the narration follow the old lunar calendar, and “I think” is this channel's view.

Information as of 2026-10-20
Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated.

t001.text: You've heard it: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji!" Japan's most famous rebel line.

t002.text: The speaker was Akechi Mitsuhide; the man he attacked was Oda Nobunaga, staying at Honnō-ji.

t003.text: 300 years later, it even became a Japanese idiom.

t004.text: But here's the surprise: we went through several records of that night, and not one has this line.

t005.text: Stranger still, 59 years later, in a book presented to the shōgun, a soldier asks him first.

t006.text: Over 180 years after that, someone had him raise a whip and shout it himself.

t007.text: So today: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji." Did Mitsuhide really shout it?

t008.text: This file follows the line for 245 years to see who first wrote it down.

t009.text: I'm a researcher at the archive. First, back to that year: Tenshō 10, Japan over 400 years ago.

t010.text: Note: I draw no historical figure here as a person. A gold fan is Nobunaga;

t011.text: a dark blue helmet is Mitsuhide. Keep these two objects in mind.

t012.text: That 5th month, Nobunaga ordered Mitsuhide to lead troops west, to the Chūgoku region.

t013.text: On the 26th, he entered his Kameyama Castle.

t014.text: Next day he prayed on Mount Atago and drew lots.

t015.text: On the 28th, he held a renga gathering there.

t016.text: Meanwhile Nobunaga reached Kyoto on the 29th, lodging at Honnō-ji.

t017.text: He had only twenty or thirty attendants with him. And the main army?

t018.text: He told his army to prepare and await word; this time, they need not follow.

t019.text: On the 1st of the 6th month, Mitsuhide met four top retainers at Kameyama. Their plan?

t020.text: What they settled on: kill Nobunaga and make Mitsuhide ruler of the realm.

t021.text: That night, Mitsuhide led his army out of Kameyama.

t022.text: They didn't take the road west; they turned east, up Oinoyama.

t023.text: On the hill the road forks: right to Yamazaki and Settsu, left down to Kyoto. Which will he take?

t024.text: Mitsuhide goes left. Left means toward Kyoto, toward Honnō-ji.

t025.text: Every story today says it was this night he shouted: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji!"

t026.text: But that night, did anyone really hear him shout it?

t027.text: Nobunaga's scribe Ōta Gyūichi wrote those days into the Shinchō Kōki.

t028.text: It's the most detailed record of its time; but that night, he wasn't there.

t029.text: He also noted the four key retainers' names. And to the whole army, what did Mitsuhide say?

t030.text: The order he recorded for the troops: via Yamazaki, march to Settsu.

t031.text: Four months later, Ōmura Yūko, Hideyoshi's writer, wrote one too. Any announcement in it?

t032.text: No. It only says Mitsuhide marched from Kameyama; no announcement.

t033.text: Instead it brands him first: not a whim, but long-held treason.

t034.text: A reminder: this was written by the winning side.

t035.text: And the report missionary Luís Fróis sent to his church?

t036.text: We read Tokutomi Sohō's Japanese translation; Tokutomi warns much of it is doubtful.

t037.text: It says Mitsuhide told the troops: Nobunaga wants to see our ranks.

t038.text: Some in the ranks grew suspicious: were they secretly sent after Tokugawa Ieyasu?

t039.text: Three records, three versions, and none has "The enemy is at Honnō-ji."

t040.text: The scribe was absent, the writer sided with the winner. What did the marchers say?

t041.text: One of them did. His name was Honjō Sōemon, and that night he marched in Mitsuhide's column.

t042.text: In Kan'ei 17, in his 80s or 90s, he wrote down that night, 58 years later.

t043.text: Its origins are unknown and it only surfaced in 1930, so we treat it as one man's memory.

t044.text: He wrote: we thought we were heading for Yamazaki, but were told Kyoto.

t045.text: Lord Ieyasu was in Kyoto then, so we only thought: Ieyasu.

t046.text: He says he didn't even know where Honnō-ji was. So what did he remember?

t047.text: What he remembered: following Saitō Toshimitsu's son; Toshimitsu was one of those four retainers.

t048.text: Downhill they went; crossing the Katsura, dawn was near.

t049.text: The Kawasumi Taikōki, written around the 1620s, covers what followed the Katsura. What did the ranks hear?

t050.text: It says the word passed along: from today our lord rules the realm, so even sandal bearers rejoice.

t051.text: But note: this order still has no "enemy," and no Honnō-ji.

t052.text: So when was Honnō-ji finally spoken aloud?

t053.text: Near Kyoto, Toshimitsu had the ward gates pushed open and the units fan out. Heading where?

t054.text: Toshimitsu said: aim for Honnō-ji's grove.

t055.text: Recall: the veteran didn't know where Honnō-ji was. At Kyoto, it was pointed out.

t056.text: But this line has no "enemy," and Mitsuhide didn't say it.

t057.text: So we can't claim the soldiers never knew whom they'd attack.

t058.text: In Honnō-ji now: only Nobunaga, those 20 or 30 pages, and a few servants.

t059.text: By daybreak, Honnō-ji was completely surrounded.

t060.text: At first Nobunaga thought servants were quarreling; at the shouts and gunfire, he asked: who's rebelling?

t061.text: Mori Ran, his page: likely Akechi's. Nobunaga said only: "Ze hi ni oyobazu."

t062.text: Our reading: it's come to this; no more to say.

t063.text: Strange: that night's one sourced famous line is Nobunaga's, not Mitsuhide's.

t064.text: Tenshō 10, month 6, day 2: Nobunaga died in the temple.

t065.text: None of those records noted Mitsuhide's line. So who first wrote it into a book?

t066.text: The earliest we've found is the book for the shōgun I mentioned: the Oda Nobunaga-fu.

t067.text: It ends: by the shōgun's order, begun early in the 11th month, presented on the 7th of the 12th.

t068.text: A whole book in just over a month. That was Kan'ei 18, 59 years after that night.

t069.text: Signed by shogunate Confucian Hayashi Razan; drafted by his son Shunsai.

t070.text: It calls Ieyasu "Daigongen." Father and son writing Oda history for the Tokugawa: how would they paint Mitsuhide?

t071.text: We didn't see the shōgun's copy; we read the Kyoto printing of Meireki 4, 17 years later.

t072.text: Here, at the renga gathering, Mitsuhide suddenly asks: how deep is Honnō-ji's moat?

t073.text: Then he eats chimaki, leaves and all. Ever forgotten to peel one?

t074.text: Neither appears in the renga gathering the Shinchō Kōki describes.

t075.text: Then Mitsuhide secretly summons retainers at Kameyama. Remember the four? Here, they become five.

t076.text: He asks the five: will you die for me? If not, cut off my head.

t077.text: Samanosuke answers first: I obey. What reason does Mitsuhide give?

t078.text: Nobunaga means to kill me. Toshimitsu says no; Samanosuke: it's been said, hurry to Kyoto.

t079.text: Leaving, he orders: enter Kyoto tomorrow morning; show Nobunaga our ranks.

t080.text: The review the missionary heard is here too.

t081.text: At Ōeyama, puzzled soldiers ask: where are we actually going?

t082.text: Mitsuhide answers: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji." Only then did all know he'd rebelled.

t083.text: In the books we found, this is the first time it has a speaker, a place, and listeners.

t084.text: Did you notice? Here, someone asks first, then he speaks.

t085.text: Over 180 years later, Rai San'yō's Nihon Gaishi wrote the scene again.

t086.text: Bunsei 10, month 5, he wrote Matsudaira Sadanobu: 20-plus years of work,

t087.text: kept boxed, unseen; Sadanobu sent for it.

t088.text: And his version of that night? A new pretext: not a review, but orders west to support Hideyoshi.

t089.text: At night they crossed Ōeyama to Oinosaka.

t090.text: Recall the opening fork? This book says right is the road to Bitchū.

t091.text: Mitsuhide turns his horse left, and the soldiers are startled. This time, does anyone ask?

t092.text: No one asks. They cross the Katsura, the river the veteran crossed near dawn.

t093.text: Mitsuhide raises his whip, points east. What does he cry out this time?

t094.text: "Waga teki wa Honnō-ji ni ari": my enemy is at Honnō-ji. That's the line everyone remembers today.

t095.text: The renga scene where he asks how deep the moat is: here too. "Only then did all know he'd rebelled" is almost identical. So what changed?

t096.text: Remember the 1641 book? There, the line was said at Ōeyama;

t097.text: here it moves to the Katsura; the answer becomes a proclamation, and gains "my" and an emphatic ending.

t098.text: Is there a link between the books? The Nihon Gaishi's source list names the Oda Nobunaga-fu.

t099.text: We can't confirm San'yō made the list; it's only circumstantial. And the self-defense motive?

t100.text: The same volume has Mitsuhide ask if his men will die for him, saying Nobunaga nearly killed him many times.

t101.text: "Nobunaga will kill me" is already in the Oda Nobunaga-fu; San'yō didn't invent it.

t102.text: So he mainly changed the scene around the line. I think that scene is just what it lacked.

t103.text: An answer to a question, or a cry with whip raised: which would you remember?

t104.text: The story isn't over. The Nihon Gaishi became the most-read history book from the Bakumatsu to Meiji.

t105.text: The National Diet Library alone has over 20 Meiji editions with this line.

t106.text: Open any one, and it's the whip-raising line. So where did it end up?

t107.text: It entered everyday Japanese: by Meiji 28, a book used it as an idiom,

t108.text: meaning: the real target lies elsewhere.

t109.text: 20 years later, even a book on world politics used it: the real enemy is Britain.

t110.text: In Japanese today, it can have nothing to do with Honnō-ji.

t111.text: And how did Meiji textbooks teach the scene?

t112.text: Both versions remain: in a Meiji 25 book, Mitsuhide shouts, whip raised;

t113.text: in a Meiji 35 textbook, the soldiers ask first, then he answers.

t114.text: So one line has two fathers. I think it's neat: its real author, too, lies elsewhere.

t115.text: Back to the opening question: who wrote "The enemy is at Honnō-ji"?

t116.text: It was written later; the earliest we've found is by Hayashi Razan and son.

t117.text: Recall the record that judged Mitsuhide four months on? The motive question started then.

t118.text: After over 400 years, motive theories are so many someone sorted them into 50 types;

t119.text: grudge, ambition, the Shikoku situation: has any become the settled answer?

t120.text: No. Letters published in 2014 spotlighted the Shikoku theory, but don't say outright why he rebelled.

t121.text: I think what turned left at the fork that night was an army; what kept walking on afterward was this line.

t122.text: So the line's case: filed. The motive's case: still open.

t123.text: Comment below: where did you first hear "The enemy is at Honnō-ji"?

t124.text: We only tell what the records show. Want to open files with us? Subscribe.
